data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive 'critical preference' grounded in risk-minimization and verisimilitude, but accepting this defense costs the agent any rational assurance of future success, reducing scientific action to a gamble on the theory that has so far best withstood falsification without implying it will continue to do so.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the distinction between 'risk-minimization based on past tests' and 'inductive inference of future reliability' collapses under logical scrutiny.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude is proven logically incoherent (as argued by Tich\u00fd and Miller), removing the basis for claiming one theory is 'closer to truth'.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the act of choosing a theory for future action inherently presupposes the uniformity of nature, regardless of the agent's stated intent.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument distinguishes between 'induction' (inferring future truth from past success) and 'critical preference' (selecting the theory that currently possesses the highest content and has survived the most severe tests). The mechanism relies on Popper's concept of verisimilitude: while we cannot know a theory is true, the one that has survived severe tests is arguably closer to the truth than its falsified rivals. Acting on it is not a prediction of future reliability but a methodological rule to minimize the risk of acting on a known falsehood. The preference is rational because it utilizes all available critical knowledge, even if that knowledge cannot guarantee future outcomes.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
